Thursday, 10 August, six in the morning. Lyon-Saint-Exupéry airport. The whole family is leaving for Romania for the christening. Hélène hasn’t flown for forty years.
Hélène, you look wonderful! Have you had your hair cut?
Yesterday. I had the hairdresser come to the care home. You don’t go to a christening with an old lady’s hairdo.
Right, I’ve had a wheelchair booked for you, as the doctor asked. It’s waiting for you at check-in.
A wheelchair! I can walk perfectly well. But fine… I’ll let myself be pushed, to please Odile.
And your suitcase? Are you checking it in, or keeping it with you?
I’m checking it in. But this little bag I’m keeping. There’s a present in it for your grandmother. I had it made specially.
A surprise. But I can tell you I had it embroidered by the best embroiderer in the Croix-Rousse.
Look, Julien is waving. Our flight is on the board: gate 23, stopover in Munich. Boarding starts in an hour.
An hour! They always make us wait at airports. In 1985 it was already like that.
A little. But Odile made me promise not to look out of the window during take-off. And Radu made me learn three Romanian songs to pass the time.
(laughs) Whatever you do, don’t let him sing on the plane. He sings out of tune.
Too late. He already made me practise "La mulți ani" in the taxi. The driver nearly made us get out.
Then let me push your wheelchair, and let’s go. Romania is waiting for us!

"Fair-fair": both "faire"s are pronounced the same, without a pause.
"Ahn-bar-kuh-mahn": two nasal "ahn"s, at the start and at the end.
"Ew-blo": the h is silent, and so is the final t.
"A-tay-reer": two r’s, one in the middle, one at the end.
1. Faire + infinitive: getting someone else to do it
When you don’t do the action yourself, but get (or pay) someone else to do it, you use FAIRE + INFINITIVE. English says "to have something done", "to get someone to…" or "to make someone…":
I had the hairdresser come. (I sent for her)
The driver nearly made us get out.
Typical mistake: "J’ai réparé ma voiture" means YOU repaired it YOURSELF. If you took it to a garage: "J’ai FAIT réparer ma voiture."
2. Se faire + infinitive: something is done to you
With a reflexive verb, "se faire + infinitive" means that someone else does the action TO you:
In the passé composé, the participle "fait" stays INVARIABLE in the causative construction: "Elle s’est FAIT couper les cheveux" (not "faite").
The object pronoun goes before FAIRE, not before the infinitive:
In the affirmative imperative, the pronoun comes after: "Fais-le entrer !" = Show him in!
"Laisser + infinitive" means "to let someone do something". As with "faire", the pronoun goes before "laisser":
The difference: "Je le fais chanter" = I make him sing (I force him). "Je le laisse chanter" = I let him sing (I don’t stop him).
The sentence you hear most: "Les passagers du vol AF 1234 sont priés de se présenter porte 23." = Passengers on flight… are requested to go to gate 23.

The plane landed in Iași in the late afternoon, after a stopover in Munich where Radu had managed to make the whole staff at the boarding gate laugh. Hélène had kept her eyes closed during take-off, as she had promised Odile. During the landing, on the other hand, she had looked out of the window without blinking.

"So this is Romania," she murmured, seeing the green hills and the red roofs. "Henri always told me he wanted to see the East. He never went. So I’m going for him." Odile squeezed her hand without saying anything.

Dan was waiting for them at the exit, with two cars borrowed from neighbours. He had had both cars washed for the occasion and had put on a tie, despite the thirty degrees. He shook the hand of each French person, saying "Bonjour, bienvenue" with an accent he had clearly been practising for weeks.

The village was forty kilometres away. On the road, Hélène wanted to see everything: carts pulled by horses, wooden wells, old women sitting on benches in front of their houses, with headscarves on. "It’s like the France of my childhood," she said, moved.

The grandmother was waiting at the gate of the house, in an embroidered blouse, surrounded by the whole family and a good part of the village. When Hélène got out of the car, the two old ladies looked at each other for a long moment. Then they embraced, very tightly, without a word, as on that first day on the bench in Lyon.

The grandmother had been getting everything ready for weeks. She had had the guest room repainted in blue, Hélène’s favourite colour, according to Ioana. She had had chairs brought from all the neighbours for the meal. And she had cooked enough sarmale to feed an army.

In the evening, under the big walnut tree behind the house, the one where Julien had asked Ioana to marry him two years earlier, Hélène took out her little bag. She handed the grandmother a parcel wrapped in tissue paper. Radu sat between them to translate.

It was a white tablecloth, embroidered with blue and red thread. In the centre, the Croix-Rousse embroiderer had depicted a bench under a lime tree, and the silhouettes of two old ladies sitting side by side. Underneath, in very fine letters, were two words: "Dor" and "Merci".

The grandmother ran her fingers over the letters for a long time. Then she stood up, went into the house and came back with something in her arms: an ie, a traditional blouse, embroidered by hand. "It was my mother who embroidered it," she said. "I was keeping it for an occasion. The occasion is you."

On the morning of 15 August, the whole house woke at dawn. Ioana had her hair done by her mother, as on her wedding day. Manon had her make-up done by Lucia. Pierre and Dan, who had no language in common, were each poured a small glass of țuică by the grandmother, "for courage", and they clinked glasses, laughing.

Hélène appeared last, in the embroidered ie, with her wedding hat. Everyone fell silent. She did a little twirl, like a young girl. "Well?" she asked. "Do I look like a Romanian?" The grandmother replied something that Radu refused to translate, blushing.

The little wooden church was full. It was hot, and the air smelled of incense and wax. Karim was holding a large candle decorated with white ribbons and did everything the priest made him do, with the seriousness of a pupil on exam day. Leïla was holding Rose-Hélène, who was looking wide-eyed at the gilded icons.

At the most important moment, the priest took the baby and dipped her three times in the water. Rose-Hélène let out a cry so powerful that the birds flew off the bell tower. In the church, everyone laughed. Hélène, in the front row, said to Odile: "She has character. She gets that from me."

Then the priest had the godparents, the baby and the parents walk three times around the altar. Karim, concentrating hard, nearly set fire to Leïla’s veil with his candle. This time it was Radu who put out the flame, with a handkerchief, blowing very hard. "Everyone gets their turn," he murmured to Karim.

After the ceremony, the meal began in the courtyard, under the trees, at long tables covered with white tablecloths. In the centre of the main table, the grandmother had spread out Hélène’s tablecloth, with the bench and the lime tree. She wouldn’t let anyone put a glass on it.

They ate for four hours. Sarmale, ciorbă, plăcinte, cozonac. Pierre, the baker, tasted the grandmother’s bread and asked her for the recipe through three interpreters. She refused to give it to him. "A family secret," Radu translated. "She’ll only tell it to Rose-Hélène."

Towards evening, the village musicians arrived: an accordion, a violin and a double bass. Lucia took out her guitar and joined them, and for an hour you could hear an incredible mixture of flamenco and Moldavian music. Nobody quite knew any more which language they were singing in.

Then Julien went over to the accordionist and hummed a tune in his ear. The old man nodded, tried a few notes, then played. It was Henri’s waltz. The violin followed, then the double bass. In the courtyard, the conversations stopped one by one.

Hélène closed her eyes. She listened to the end, her hands folded on her knees. Then, as the last note was fading, the grandmother stood up and held out her hand to her. "Acum, hora," she said. There was no need for a translation.

The musicians struck up a hora. Everyone stood up and joined hands to form a big circle: the Romanians, the French, the Spanish girl, the godparents Karim and Leïla, and in the middle, on a chair brought specially, Hélène, clapping her hands and laughing.

On the second round she couldn’t hold back any longer. She stood up, despite Odile’s protests, and joined the circle, between the grandmother and Ioana. She didn’t know the steps. She didn’t need to. She let herself be carried by the music and by the hands holding her on each side.

Julien was holding Rose-Hélène in his arms, a little apart, and he watched the scene unable to speak. Two old ladies, one from Lyon, the other from Moldavia, who had never exchanged a single sentence in the same language, were dancing the hora hand in hand, under a walnut tree, to the sound of an old accordion.

That evening, once the party was over and the last lanterns were out, Hélène sat down on the bench by the gate, next to the grandmother. They stayed there a long time looking at the stars, without talking. Now and then, one would say a word in her own language, and the other would nod, as if she had understood.

Before going to bed, Ioana came to bring them blankets. She heard Hélène say softly, in Romanian, with her terrible accent: "Mulțumesc, prietena mea." And the grandmother reply, in French, with an even worse accent: "Merci, mon amie." They had each learned the other’s language in secret. Ioana never found out who had got them to learn.

Odile has made a list for the trip. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
Monday: I had the passports checked. Hélène’s had expired in 1993! We had a new one made urgently, in three days.
Tuesday: I had a vaccination, as a precaution. Hélène refused. "At my age," she said, "it’s the germs that are afraid of me."
Wednesday: I had my blue dress cleaned for the christening. Hélène had her hair cut. She let the hairdresser decide on the style, which is a miracle.
Thursday: up at four. I called a taxi. Radu made everyone sing. The driver nearly made us get out on the motorway.
Don’t forget: don’t let Hélène carry her suitcase. Don’t let Radu buy sarmale at the airport, because of customs. He’s already had a jar confiscated in Corsica.
And above all: get Julien to take lots of photos. I want to show Isabelle that at seventy-eight her mother still sets off on adventures.
